precepts.text: A king sealed the den with his own signet so the decree could not be changed, showing the binding authority of a royal seal.
precepts.point: She commanded them to proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high, and set two sons of Belial before him to bear false witness that he blasphemed God and the king, then stone him. This was evil counsel and a murderous plot.

note.label: 1 Kings 21: Naboth's Vineyard and the Judgment on Ahab

precepts.why:
“And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that the purpose might not be changed concerning Daniel.” A king sealed the den with his own signet so the decree could not be changed. That is the binding authority of a royal seal.

Jezebel “wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal”. The seal was a signet, the official mark of the king’s authority, so when those letters reached the elders and nobles of Naboth’s city, they carried royal weight as if Ahab himself had written them.

precepts.text: Paul exercised himself to always have a conscience void of offence toward God and toward men, just as Daniel did.
precepts.point: This is how our forefathers rolled, and the same kind of spirit we should be rolling in. They concluded they could only find something against him concerning the law of his God.

note.label: Daniel 6: Daniel in the Den of Lions

precepts.why:
“And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.” Paul exercised himself at it, worked at it, so that neither God nor men could find offence in him. That is exactly what Daniel did. The presidents and princes sought occasion against him concerning the kingdom, “but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.” He was blameless: void of offence toward men in the affairs of the kingdom, and void of offence toward God in keeping his law.

The only thing left for them to try was the law of his God: “We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.” There was nothing else on him.

This is how our forefathers rolled, and the same kind of spirit we should be rolling in: exercising ourselves, as Daniel and Paul did, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God and toward men.

precepts.text: When a man's ways please the Most High, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him; Daniel was operating in a righteous spirit.
precepts.point: The king was glad and commanded Daniel taken up, and no manner of hurt was found on him because he believed in his God; then the accusers, their children, and wives were cast in and the lions brake their bones before they reached the bottom.

note.label: Daniel 6: Daniel in the Den of Lions

precepts.why:
“When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.” Daniel's ways pleased the Lord, and so even the lions were at peace with him: “My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me”. Daniel was operating in a righteous spirit, innocent before God, and “before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.”

The king was exceeding glad and commanded Daniel taken up out of the den, and “no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God.” The same lions that were at peace with Daniel had the mastery of his accusers, their children, and their wives, and brake all their bones in pieces before they came to the bottom of the den. The difference was not the lions; it was whose ways pleased the Lord.
